title: The Art of Delegation
author: Ian Hallett
source: The Art of Leadership series (ianhallett.com), August 15, 2026
summary: Ian Hallett, in this installment of his Art of Leadership series, argues that most discussions of delegation confuse two fundamentally different acts: distributing work, which is safe because the leader retains every decision, and distributing authority, which requires accepting that decisions will sometimes be made differently, and occasionally worse, than the leader would have made them. He cites a 2021 Journal of Organization Design study linking chief executives' measured personal dominance to narrower delegation of decision rights, arguing the failure to distribute authority is often a matter of temperament rather than a fixable skills gap, and that this tendency intensifies rather than softens as leaders gain more power. Drawing on psychological ownership research, Hallett argues that capable employees given responsibility without matching authority quickly learn their judgment isn't trusted and leave for organizations that will let them decide, making authority-hoarding a retention risk as much as a bottleneck problem. His practical recommendation is to begin delegation not with tasks but with an organization's recurring decisions (pricing exceptions, hiring approvals, refunds), naming a single owner and explicit boundaries for each, while the harder discipline is resisting the urge to reclaim authority the first time a delegated decision turns out differently than the leader would have chosen. He closes with a specific self-diagnostic: auditing which decisions genuinely required the leader's involvement over a two-week period versus which arrived only because no one below had been given permission to decide, arguing the second category is typically far larger and measures authority withheld rather than work undone.
points: Hallett's central distinction, that delegating tasks is safe while delegating authority means accepting 'the right to be wrong,' reframes why leaders can distribute enormous amounts of work while still functioning as an organizational bottleneck.

The 2021 Journal of Organization Design finding linking CEO personal dominance to narrower delegation of decision rights supports his claim that authority-hoarding is often a temperament issue, not a fixable process gap, and worsens as power increases.

He frames authority-hoarding as a retention risk, not just an efficiency problem: capable employees who sense their judgment isn't trusted will leave for organizations that let them decide, regardless of their title.

His practical delegation method starts with an organization's recurring decisions (pricing exceptions, hiring approvals, refunds) rather than tasks, assigning a named owner and explicit escalation boundaries to each.

The two-week decision audit, sorting incoming decisions into those that genuinely needed the leader versus those that arrived only because no one below had permission to decide, gives leaders a concrete diagnostic for measuring authority withheld rather than work undone.
quotes: Delegation is commonly understood as the distribution of work. Its harder and more consequential form is handing over authority, and the two are not the same thing.

Authority is different because it transfers the right to be wrong. To delegate a decision is to accept that it may be made differently from how the leader would have made it, and occasionally made badly, without the matter returning for correction.
the authors found that more dominant chief executives maintained a significantly wider personal span of control and delegated fewer decision rights than their less dominant counterparts.
A talented person given a title but not the authority that should accompany it learns quickly that their judgment is not trusted, and that the interesting decisions will always be made elsewhere.

Delegation fails when leaders reclaim authority at the first sign of discomfort. The instinct to intervene is strongest precisely when intervention is most damaging, because a reasonable decision taken independently is often worth more to an organisation than a marginally better one that reinforces its dependence on a single person.

The organisations that outgrow their founders are not those whose leaders learned to distribute tasks more efficiently. They are those whose leaders learned to distribute the right to decide, and then, at the first uncomfortable test of that decision, declined to take it back.
